title: Before Socrates
tagline: The philosopher who dared say the sun is a rock, not a god.

scenes.text: The Greek world, 5th century BCE. Before Socrates asked 'How should we live?', other thinkers had already asked harder questions: What is the universe made of? Can motion truly exist? Are our senses trustworthy? Two thinkers push these questions to their breaking point.

scenes.speaker: Anaxagoras
scenes.text: The sun is not a god. It is a burning rock, perhaps the size of the Peloponnese. The moon reflects light it borrows from the sun. Look up and you will see not divinity — but matter, in motion, following laws.
This statement nearly got Anaxagoras executed in Athens. The friend and teacher of Pericles, he was tried for impiety and exiled — a reminder that even then, new ideas were dangerous.

challenge.fact: Around 450 BCE, Anaxagoras was charged with impiety for saying the sun was a fiery rock larger than the Peloponnese. He was saved from execution by his friend Pericles but exiled from Athens.

challenge.instruction: Anaxagoras was put on trial in Athens for claiming the sun was a fiery rock, not a divine being. The way to the answer runs through these passages — find the exit.

scenes.speaker: Zeno of Elea
scenes.text: Consider Achilles racing a tortoise. Give the tortoise a head start. Achilles must first reach where the tortoise was. But by then the tortoise has moved. Achilles must reach that new point. But the tortoise has moved again. Logically — he can never catch it.

scenes.speaker: Anaxagoras
scenes.text: And yet we observe that he does catch it. So where is the error in your reasoning?

scenes.speaker: Zeno of Elea
scenes.text: That is precisely my point. Our reasoning contradicts our senses, or our senses contradict our reason. One of them is lying. I trust reason.

challenge.instruction: Anaxagoras estimated the sun's size using shadows and geometry. Calculate the sun's angle from shadow measurements.
challenge.fact: Anaxagoras correctly deduced that the moon shines with reflected sunlight, that eclipses occur when the moon covers the sun, and that the sun is a glowing rock. All this 2,500 years before telescopes.

scenes.text: Zeno's paradoxes tormented philosophers for two thousand years. They were only resolved when Newton and Leibniz invented calculus — the mathematics of infinite sums — in the 17th century.

challenge.instruction: Anaxagoras held that Nous (Mind) imposes order on chaos — each element in its proper place. Fill the grid so each row, column, and 2×2 box contains 1–4 exactly once.
challenge.fact: Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was the first to introduce Nous — cosmic Mind — as the ordering principle of the universe. He correctly deduced that the moon shines with reflected sunlight and that eclipses are caused by the moon blocking the sun.
The pre-Socratics were the first to explain nature without myth. Their debate between flux (Heraclitus) and permanence (Parmenides) set up every major argument in Western philosophy that followed.

Anaxagoras said the sun is a fiery rock that lights the moon. Prove it — use one mirror to route sunlight across three reflections and illuminate the far corner.
challenge.fact: Anaxagoras was the first to correctly explain lunar phases and eclipses: the moon reflects the sun's light and the earth's shadow causes eclipses. He deduced this by reasoning about light and geometry, 2,500 years before anyone could test it directly.

challenge.instruction: Restore Homer's opening to the Iliad — the invocation of the Muse and the quarrel that sets ten years of war in motion.
challenge.fact: Homer's Iliad, composed around 750 BCE, was the closest thing ancient Greeks had to a sacred text. Alexander the Great slept with an annotated copy under his pillow, alongside a dagger. The poem covers only 51 days of the decade-long Trojan War, yet captures the whole arc of human conflict.
